introduction.text: The Caserma dei Vigili is a Roman barracks in Ostia that housed a cohort of fire‑fighting soldiers. It illustrates the military and civic infrastructure of the ancient port and shows how the imperial cult and everyday life were integrated into a single complex.

history.description: The barracks was rebuilt in the Adriatic period (132‑137 CE) to accommodate a cohort of vigiles from Rome.
In the Severan period (205 CE) a second detachment was stationed at Porto, and the Ostian barracks was expanded with new tabernae and an imperial cult precinct.
The Ostian detachment probably ceased to operate in the mid‑3rd century, while the Porto detachment continued until the late 4th century.

design.description: The building is rectangular, surrounding a large courtyard paved with bipedali and surrounded by a portico of brick pillars. The eastern entrance features a stone portal with a vestibule.
The western side contains a row of tabernae added in the 2nd century, with a central staircase to upper floors.
A western corridor in the Adriatic phase ends with a bath‑like basin, and the imperial cult area includes a pronaos with marble columns and a mosaic floor.

art.description: Mosaic floors in the courtyard and in the imperial cult area feature geometric patterns and scenes of sacrifice, including a bull and a flautist.
Statue bases in the cult precinct honor emperors such as Antoninus Pius, Lucius Verus, Septimius Severus, Marcus Aurelius, and Caracalla.
Graffiti on walls record the names of vigiles, their ranks, and thank‑you inscriptions to the reigning emperor.
